sections.title: Simple and complex extensions
sections.summary: Simple extensions carry a single value[x]. Complex extensions nest child extensions to represent structured additional data. Both require a defining StructureDefinition and canonical URL.
keyPoints: Simple: url + one value[x]
Complex: url + child extension elements
Prefer reuse of published extensions
Complex extensions still must declare context
Do not reinvent elements that already exist in the base resource
sections.examTip: If you need multiple fields under one extension, you likely need a complex extension.
sections.detail:
Slide 1: Simple extension

One defining url and one value[x] (valueString, valueCodeableConcept, valueBoolean, and so on).

Slide 2: Complex extension

Parent extension URL plus nested extensions for each sub-field (for example latitude/longitude components).

Slide 3: Design preference order

  1. Use existing base elements
  2. Use a registered extension
  3. Define a governed local extension only if needed

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish simple vs complex by whether one value is enough or a nested structure is required.

sections.title: Modifier extensions
sections.summary: ModifierExtension is an extension that qualifies or changes the meaning of the element or resource. Receivers that do not understand a modifier must not process the resource as if the modifier were absent.
keyPoints: Appears in modifierExtension arrays, not extension arrays
Changes interpretation—safety critical
Unknown modifiers ⇒ refuse or fail safely
Never copy resources while silently dropping modifiers
Some core elements are also isModifier=true without being extensions
sections.examTip: “Ignore unknown extensions” is wrong when the unknown item is a modifierExtension.
sections.detail:
Slide 1: Definition

modifierExtension: An extension that modifies the meaning of its context.

It is not optional decoration.

Slide 2: Handling rule

A system must understand the modifier or refuse safe processing.

Silent ignore is a classic exam trap.

Slide 3: Practical examples

Think of modifiers as “this statement is negated/qualified/altered”—processing without that qualifier is wrong.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Correct answer almost always emphasizes understand or refuse.

sections.title: Finding and reusing registered extensions
sections.summary: Before defining a new extension, search HL7, FHIR Extension Registry patterns, and relevant IGs (US Core, Da Vinci) for an existing definition you can reuse.
keyPoints: Reuse improves interoperability and validation support
IG packages already include many US-needed extensions
Match extension context to your element path
Pinned package versions keep extension definitions stable
Local duplicates of registered extensions create mapping debt
sections.examTip: Exam and real projects both reward reuse of published extensions over bespoke clones.
sections.detail:
Slide 1: Search before inventing

Check base FHIR extension documentation and your target IG’s defined extensions first.

Slide 2: Why reuse wins

  • Shared meaning across partners
  • Existing StructureDefinitions for validation
  • Fewer custom governance battles

Slide 3: Adoption checklist

  1. Find candidate extension
  2. Confirm context and cardinality
  3. Add package dependency
  4. Populate the canonical URL correctly

Slide 4: Exam focus

Prefer “use the registered extension” over “define a new local extension” when both seem possible.

sections.title: Extension context and canonical URL
sections.summary: Every extension definition includes a canonical URL and context rules describing where it may appear (resource, datatype, or element path). Wrong URL or wrong context fails conformance.
keyPoints: Canonical URL uniquely identifies the extension definition
Context can be FHIRPath/element path based
Using an extension outside its context is invalid
Instance extension.url must match the definition canonical
Versioning of extension definitions follows package/IG governance
sections.examTip: If validation says wrong context, your extension may be legally defined but placed on the wrong element.
sections.detail:
Slide 1: Canonical URL

The extension’s url in the instance must equal the StructureDefinition canonical that defines it.

Slide 2: Context

Context: Where the extension is allowed—for example on Patient, on Address, or on a specific element path.

Slide 3: Failure modes

  • Typo in URL
  • Using a Patient extension on Encounter
  • Missing package so validator cannot resolve URL

Slide 4: Exam focus

Correct extension use = right canonical + right context + right value type.

Document cardinality, value types, and examples

description: Model identity, organizations, locations, encounters, roles, and administrative relationships.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Core demographic elements

The Patient resource carries demographics in dedicated elements: name (HumanName, repeatable with a use code such as official/usual/nickname), gender (administrative-gender: male | female | other | unknown), birthDate, address, and deceased[x] (boolean or dateTime).

Patient.gender is explicitly an administrative concept used for record-matching and clinical algorithms-not a statement of biological sex or gender identity.

Slide 2: Identifiers

identifier is a repeatable Identifier datatype: system (a URI naming the assigning authority, e.g. an OID or a hospital's namespace) plus value (the actual MRN, SSN, or national ID).

  • identifier.use - usual | official | temp | secondary | old
  • identifier.type - CodeableConcept from the Identifier Type Codes value set (e.g. MR for medical record number, SS for SSN)
  • identifier.assigner - Reference(Organization) that issued it

Slide 3: Multiple births and search

multipleBirth[x] can be boolean (was part of a multiple birth) or integer (birth order).

Common search parameters: identifier, name, family, given, birthdate, gender, address. Matching on identifier + name + birthDate is the standard patient-matching pattern.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect a distractor equating gender with biological sex, and questions on which Identifier sub-elements (system vs value vs type) hold which piece of an MRN/SSN.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: telecom - contact points

Patient.telecom is 0..* ContactPoint: system (phone | fax | email | pager | url | sms | other), value, use (home | work | temp | old | mobile), and rank for ordering preference.

Multiple telecoms are common-e.g. a mobile phone ranked 1 and a work email ranked 2.

Slide 2: communication - language preference

Patient.communication (BackboneElement, 0..*): language (CodeableConcept, extensible binding to BCP-47 codes such as en-US or es) and preferred (boolean).

Only one entry should be marked preferred = true; this drives interpreter and materials-translation workflows.

Slide 3: contact - related persons

Patient.contact (BackboneElement) captures a person tied to the patient for communication purposes: relationship, name, telecom, address, gender, organization, period.

This is distinct from the RelatedPerson resource, which is used when that person needs to be a first-class subject of other resources (e.g. as a Coverage subscriber).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish telecom (how to reach the patient), communication (spoken/written language needs), and contact (a related person's details embedded in Patient).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Practitioner - the person

Practitioner represents an individual person, independent of any specific role: identifier (e.g. a US National Provider Identifier/NPI), name, telecom, address, gender, birthDate, photo, and communication (languages spoken).

Slide 2: qualification

Practitioner.qualification (BackboneElement, 0..*): identifier, code (CodeableConcept for the credential, e.g. MD, board certification), period (validity), and issuer (Reference(Organization)).

This models licenses and certifications tied to the person, not to a specific job.

Slide 3: PractitionerRole - the working relationship

PractitionerRole is a separate resource linking a practitioner to an organization, one or more locations, and healthcareServices for a defined period.

Splitting person from role means the same Practitioner can have several PractitionerRole resources (e.g. moonlighting at two hospitals).

Slide 4: Exam focus

A frequent trap: putting specialty or organization directly on Practitioner. In R4, those belong on PractitionerRole.

sections.title: Identity and qualifications
sections.examTip: Remember Practitioner holds the person's qualifications; role, specialty, and organization affiliation live on PractitionerRole.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: code vs specialty

PractitionerRole.code (CodeableConcept, example binding to Practitioner Role codes) describes the practitioner's functional role-e.g. doctor, nurse, pharmacist.

PractitionerRole.specialty (CodeableConcept, example binding, often populated with taxonomy codes such as US NUCC) describes the clinical specialty-e.g. cardiology, general practice, dermatology.

Slide 2: Scoping the role

  • practitioner - Reference(Practitioner) being described
  • organization - Reference(Organization) the role is performed for
  • location - Reference(Location)[] where the role is performed
  • healthcareService - Reference(HealthcareService)[] offered in this role
  • period - the active date range of this role

Slide 3: Multiple roles per practitioner

A single practitioner can have several PractitionerRole resources-e.g. "cardiologist at Hospital A" and "general practitioner at Clinic B"-each with its own code, specialty, organization, and location.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect an item asking which element (code vs specialty) is the right place to record "cardiologist" versus "attending physician."

slides.title: code vs specialty
slides.body:

specialty is the clinical area (e.g. cardiology, nephrology)
both are CodeableConcepts with example bindings

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Endpoint resource

Endpoint models a technical connection point for exchanging data: status (active | suspended | error | off | entered-in-error | test), connectionType (e.g. hl7-fhir-rest, hl7-fhir-msg, ihe-xcpd, dicom-wado-rs), address (the actual URL), payloadType, and payloadMimeType.

Organization, Location, HealthcareService, and PractitionerRole can each reference an Endpoint via their endpoint element.

Slide 2: HealthcareService availability

HealthcareService.availableTime (BackboneElement): daysOfWeek, allDay, availableStartTime, availableEndTime-models a recurring weekly schedule.

notAvailable (description + during Period) captures planned closures, and availabilityExceptions is free text for anything not otherwise structured.

Slide 3: Location hours and service details

Location.hoursOfOperation mirrors the same daysOfWeek/openingTime/closingTime pattern for a physical site.

HealthcareService also carries appointmentRequired, eligibility, serviceProvisionCode, and coverageArea to describe how and where the service can be accessed.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Do not confuse a technical Endpoint (system-to-system connectivity) with human-facing availableTime/hoursOfOperation (when a service or location is open).

title: Essential administrative resources

description: Represent diagnoses, allergies, procedures, plans, goals, family history, and risk.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: clinicalStatus

Condition.clinicalStatus (CodeableConcept, required binding to the Condition Clinical Status Codes value set): active, recurrence, relapse, inactive, remission, resolved.

It describes where the condition currently stands clinically, independent of how certain the diagnosis is.

Slide 2: verificationStatus

Condition.verificationStatus (CodeableConcept, required binding): unconfirmed, provisional, differential, confirmed, refuted, entered-in-error.

This tracks confidence in the diagnosis itself, separate from the clinical course captured by clinicalStatus.

Slide 3: The interaction rule

Constraint con-5: clinicalStatus SHALL NOT be present if verificationStatus is entered-in-error.

Otherwise (verificationStatus not entered-in-error), clinicalStatus is expected to be present-an erroneous record shouldn't also claim an active clinical course.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Questions often test the con-5 constraint directly: pairing entered-in-error with a populated clinicalStatus is an invalid Condition.

clinicalStatus is required unless verificationStatus is entered-in-error
the two use separate, required-strength code systems

sections.detail:
Slide 1: category

Condition.category (CodeableConcept[], example binding) classifies why the record exists: problem-list-item (an ongoing item on the patient's problem list) versus encounter-diagnosis (a diagnosis made during a specific encounter).

Slide 2: severity

Condition.severity (CodeableConcept, example binding, commonly SNOMED CT) grades clinical intensity, typically mild, moderate, or severe. It is distinct from clinicalStatus, which tracks course rather than intensity.

Slide 3: onset[x] and abatement[x]

onset[x] - dateTime, Age, Period, Range, or string; records when the condition began.

abatement[x] - dateTime, Age, Period, Range, string, or boolean; records resolution. abatementBoolean = true means resolved but without a known/recorded date.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Watch for questions asking which onset/abatement type fits a scenario (e.g. "resolved as a teenager" -> abatementAge, or "resolved, exact date unknown" -> abatementBoolean).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: code - the overall allergen

AllergyIntolerance.code (CodeableConcept, example binding) identifies the substance, product, or allergen the intolerance is against-e.g. RxNorm for a medication, SNOMED CT for a general substance like "peanut."

Slide 2: category

AllergyIntolerance.category (code[], required binding): food | medication | environment | biologic. It broadly classifies the kind of substance without pinning down the exact agent.

Slide 3: reaction.substance

Within each reaction entry, reaction.substance (CodeableConcept) can identify the specific substance that caused that particular episode-useful when it differs in specificity from the top-level code (e.g. code = "penicillin" class, reaction.substance = "amoxicillin").

Slide 4: Exam focus

Be ready to pick between the top-level code and a per-episode reaction.substance when a scenario names a specific drug that triggered one reaction.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Definition

AllergyIntolerance.criticality (code, required binding): low | high | unable-to-assess.

It estimates the potential for clinically serious harm as a result of a future exposure, including the possibility of a fatal outcome.

Slide 2: Criticality vs severity

criticality is a single, overall risk judgment about the allergy/intolerance as a whole.

reaction.severity (mild | moderate | severe) instead grades the intensity of one specific, already-observed reaction episode.

A patient could have had only a mild reaction but still be flagged high criticality if a future exposure could be life-threatening (e.g. known anaphylaxis risk).

Slide 3: unable-to-assess

unable-to-assess is used when there isn't enough clinical information to make a risk judgment yet-distinct from simply leaving criticality absent.

Slide 4: Exam focus

The classic exam trap is treating criticality and severity as synonyms-they answer different questions (future risk vs. past episode intensity).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: reaction backbone element

AllergyIntolerance.reaction (BackboneElement, 0..*) represents one clinical event/episode: it can carry its own substance, manifestation, description, onset, severity, exposureRoute, and note.

Slide 2: manifestation

reaction.manifestation (CodeableConcept, 1..*, required within the reaction) records the observed clinical signs/symptoms-e.g. urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis, rash-typically coded with SNOMED CT.

Because it is required whenever a reaction entry exists, a reaction cannot be recorded with zero manifestations.

Slide 3: Supporting detail

  • exposureRoute - how the patient was exposed (e.g. oral, topical)
  • onset - dateTime the reaction began
  • severity - mild | moderate | severe for this specific episode
  • description - free-text narrative of what happened

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know that manifestation is mandatory once a reaction is recorded, and that multiple reaction entries can exist for repeated exposures over time.

reaction.manifestation (CodeableConcept, 1..*, required within the reaction) records the observed clinical signs/symptoms-e.g. urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis, rash-typically coded with SNOMED CT.

Because it is required whenever a reaction entry exists, a reaction cannot be recorded with zero manifestations.

slides.title: Supporting detail
slides.body:
• exposureRoute - how the patient was exposed (e.g. oral, topical)
  • onset - dateTime the reaction began
  • severity - mild | moderate | severe for this specific episode
  • description - free-text narrative of what happened

slides.title: Exam focus
slides.body: Know that manifestation is mandatory once a reaction is recorded, and that multiple reaction entries can exist for repeated exposures over time.

keyPoints: reaction is 0..* - one entry per distinct exposure/episode
manifestation (1..*) lists the signs/symptoms, e.g. urticaria, anaphylaxis
reaction also carries substance, onset, severity, and exposureRoute
description and note allow free-text detail alongside coded manifestations

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Where severity lives

severity is an element of AllergyIntolerance.reaction, not of AllergyIntolerance itself. Each reaction episode can carry its own severity value.

Slide 2: Allowed values

reaction.severity (code, required binding to AllergyIntoleranceSeverity): mild, moderate, severe-a straightforward three-level clinical grading of how bad that particular episode was.

Slide 3: Severity vs criticality recap

If a patient has had two reactions-one mild rash and one severe anaphylaxis-there would be two reaction entries with different severity values, while a single top-level criticality (likely high, given the anaphylaxis history) summarizes overall future risk.

Slide 4: Exam focus

If a question describes multiple past episodes of different intensity, expect multiple reaction entries each with their own severity, not one shared value.

Slide 1: status

Procedure.status (code, required, modifier element): preparation | in-progress | not-done | on-hold | stopped | completed | entered-in-error | unknown.

Because it is a modifier, a receiving system must inspect it-e.g. a not-done Procedure describes something that did not happen and must not be treated as a completed intervention.

Slide 2: statusReason

Procedure.statusReason (CodeableConcept) explains the current status-most importantly, why a procedure is not-done (e.g. patient declined, contraindicated) or why it was stopped partway through.

Slide 3: reasonCode / reasonReference

Procedure.reasonCode (CodeableConcept[]) and reasonReference (Reference(Condition|Observation|...)[]) capture the clinical indication-why the procedure was ordered/performed in the first place, independent of its status.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect a scenario distinguishing "why wasn't it done" (statusReason on a not-done Procedure) from "why was it ordered" (reasonCode/reasonReference).

Slide 1: bodySite

Procedure.bodySite (CodeableConcept[], example binding, typically SNOMED CT body-structure codes) records where on the body the procedure was performed, e.g. "left knee" or "appendix."

Slide 2: performer

Procedure.performer (BackboneElement, 0..*): function (CodeableConcept describing the role in this procedure, e.g. surgeon, assistant, anesthetist) and actor (Reference to who/what actually performed it).

Slide 3: actor and onBehalfOf

actor can reference Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, Patient (self-performed), RelatedPerson, or Device (e.g. a robotic surgical system).

onBehalfOf (Reference(Organization)) records the organization the performer was acting for, useful for locum or contracted staff.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Multiple performers with different function values (surgeon vs. assistant) on one Procedure is a common exam scenario-know they share the same performer array with distinct function codes.

Slide 1: outcome

Procedure.outcome (CodeableConcept, example binding) gives a high-level summary of the result, e.g. "successful" or "partial success." Detailed clinical results typically live in related Observation resources instead.

Slide 2: complication and complicationDetail

Procedure.complication (CodeableConcept[]) codes any adverse events that occurred during or after the procedure.

Procedure.complicationDetail (Reference(Condition)[]) points to full Condition resources when the complication warrants a complete clinical record.

Slide 3: report and followUp

Procedure.report (Reference(DiagnosticReport | DocumentReference | Composition)[]) links to detailed documentation such as an operative note.

Procedure.followUp (CodeableConcept[]) records instructions for what should happen next, e.g. "return in 2 weeks for suture removal."

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know which element is coded-only (complication) versus which links to a full resource (complicationDetail, report) when a question asks how to represent a documented post-op infection.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: intent

CarePlan.intent (code, required binding to request-intent): proposal | plan | order | option.

This mirrors the same pattern used by MedicationRequest.intent and ServiceRequest.intent-it says how authoritative this plan is, from a loose suggestion to an actionable order.

Slide 2: CarePlan.status

CarePlan.status (required, modifier): draft | active | on-hold | revoked | completed | entered-in-error | unknown-tracks the plan's own overall lifecycle, separate from the status of any individual activity.

Slide 3: activity

CarePlan.activity (BackboneElement, 0..*) represents an action within the plan. activity.reference (Reference) typically points to the actual request resource carrying full detail (e.g. a ServiceRequest or MedicationRequest).

Where no separate resource exists, activity.detail can describe the action inline, including its own status (not-started | scheduled | in-progress | on-hold | completed | cancelled | stopped | unknown | entered-in-error).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Watch for confusing plan-level status with activity-level detail.status-a CarePlan can be active while one of its activities is individually completed.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Goal.target

Goal.target (BackboneElement, 0..*): measure (CodeableConcept naming what's tracked, often matching an Observation code such as HbA1c), detail[x] (Quantity | Range | CodeableConcept | string | boolean | integer | Ratio - the actual target value), and due[x] (date or Duration).

Multiple target entries let one Goal track several measures at once, e.g. both blood pressure and weight.

Slide 2: Goal status tracking

Goal.achievementStatus (CodeableConcept, example binding): in-progress, improving, worsening, no-change, achieved, sustaining, not-achieved, no-progress, not-attainable.

Goal.lifecycleStatus separately tracks the goal record's own state (proposed | active | completed | ...).

Slide 3: CarePlan and CareTeam

CarePlan.careTeam (Reference(CareTeam)[]) links the plan to the team responsible for carrying it out. CarePlan.goal (Reference(Goal)[]) links the plan to the Goals it pursues.

The CareTeam resource itself lists participant entries (BackboneElement): role, member (Reference(Practitioner | PractitionerRole | RelatedPerson | Patient | Organization | CareTeam)), and period.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know that a Goal's progress toward multiple measures is modeled with multiple target entries, not multiple Goal resources, and that team membership sits in CareTeam.participant, referenced from CarePlan via careTeam.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: effective[x]

Observation.effective[x]: The clinically relevant time for the observation - when the measurement or assessment applies to the patient.

Allowed types: dateTime, Period (e.g. a urine collection window), Timing, or instant.

Slide 2: issued

Observation.issued: An instant marking when this version of the observation was made available to providers, e.g. released from the lab system.

issued can be later than effective[x] - a specimen drawn Monday may not be resulted (issued) until Wednesday.

Slide 3: Why both matter

  • effective[x] drives clinical timelines and trending (e.g. vital sign charts)
  • issued supports audit trails, amendment tracking, and result-latency reporting
  • A corrected result gets a new issued time even when effective[x] is unchanged

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam items often swap these two: remember effective[x] = when it happened to the patient, issued = when the report/result was released.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Reference range

Observation.referenceRange: A backbone element giving the normal or expected range for the result - low, high, type (e.g. normal, treatment range), appliesTo (population, e.g. sex), and free-text text.

A single Observation can carry multiple referenceRange entries for different populations or contexts.

Slide 2: component for panels

Observation.component: Repeating structure for results that are always reported together but need distinct codes/values, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Each component has its own code, value[x], and may carry its own referenceRange and interpretation.

Slide 3: Panels via hasMember

  • hasMember - references other Observation resources that make up a panel (e.g. a CBC panel referencing individual differential Observations)
  • Use component when sub-results are inseparable and always reported as a unit
  • Use hasMember plus separate Observations when sub-results can stand alone or have independent lifecycles

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam scenario: choosing component vs a separate Observation linked by hasMember for panel results - pick component only when the parts are inseparable.

slides.title: Reference range
slides.body:
Observation.referenceRange: A backbone element giving the normal or expected range for the result - low, high, type (e.g. normal, treatment range), appliesTo (population, e.g. sex), and free-text text.

A single Observation can carry multiple referenceRange entries for different populations or contexts.

slides.title: component for panels
slides.body:
Observation.component: Repeating structure for results that are always reported together but need distinct codes/values, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Each component has its own code, value[x], and may carry its own referenceRange and interpretation.

slides.title: Panels via hasMember
slides.body:
• hasMember - references other Observation resources that make up a panel (e.g. a CBC panel referencing individual differential Observations)
  • Use component when sub-results are inseparable and always reported as a unit
  • Use hasMember plus separate Observations when sub-results can stand alone or have independent lifecycles

slides.title: Exam focus
slides.body: Exam scenario: choosing component vs a separate Observation linked by hasMember for panel results - pick component only when the parts are inseparable.

keyPoints: referenceRange has low, high, type, appliesTo, and text
component repeats code + value[x] + its own referenceRange
Blood pressure panel is the classic component example
hasMember links independent Observations into a panel
sections.summary: Observation.referenceRange defines normal/expected value bounds for a result, and Observation.component models multi-part results such as panels where each component has its own code, value, and reference range.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: conclusion and conclusionCode

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: Free-text clinical interpretation/impression of the report (e.g. a radiologist's summary).

DiagnosticReport.conclusionCode: Coded version of the conclusion, typically bound to SNOMED CT, giving a machine-readable diagnosis alongside the narrative.

Slide 2: presentedForm

DiagnosticReport.presentedForm: An Attachment holding the full formatted report exactly as issued - often a PDF, RTF, or scanned image.

Key Attachment fields: contentType, data (base64) or url, title, creation.

Slide 3: Using both together

  • result (references to Observation) carries structured, queryable data
  • conclusion/conclusionCode carry the coded clinical summary
  • presentedForm carries the human-readable rendered document
  • A report can legitimately include all three at once

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember: presentedForm is the rendered document; it does not substitute for structured result references or coded conclusionCode.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: intent

ServiceRequest.intent: 1..1, required binding. States the nature of the request: proposal, plan, directive, order, original-order, reflex-order, filler-order, instance-order, or option.

Most clinical orders use order; a reflex lab test triggered by a rule uses reflex-order.

Slide 2: priority

ServiceRequest.priority: 0..1, values routine, urgent, asap, stat. Defaults to routine when absent.

priority signals how quickly the request should be actioned; it does not track workflow progress.

Slide 3: intent vs status

  • status tracks workflow lifecycle: draft | active | on-hold | revoked | completed | entered-in-error | unknown
  • intent tracks the kind/level of authorization the request represents
  • Both are required, independent elements - do not conflate them

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam trap: mixing up intent (kind of request) with status (lifecycle state) or priority (urgency) - all three are distinct elements.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: reasonCode and reasonReference

ServiceRequest.reasonCode: Coded indication for why the service is being requested (e.g. a diagnosis code justifying an imaging study).

ServiceRequest.reasonReference: Reference to a Condition, Observation, DiagnosticReport, or DocumentReference that documents the reason.

Slide 2: supportingInfo

ServiceRequest.supportingInfo: 0..*, Reference(Any). Additional clinical information relevant to fulfilling the request that isn't itself the reason - e.g. recent labs, allergy notes, or relevant prior imaging.

Slide 3: Reason vs supporting info

  • reasonCode/reasonReference answer "why was this ordered?"
  • supportingInfo answers "what else should the performer know?"
  • Both help the fulfiller (e.g. a lab or imaging center) triage and interpret the order correctly

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish the justification (reasonCode/reasonReference) from contextual data (supportingInfo) attached to a ServiceRequest.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: collection

Specimen.collection: Backbone element for the collection event - collector (who), collected[x] (dateTime/Period), quantity, method, bodySite, and fastingStatus[x] (was the patient fasting).

Slide 2: processing

Specimen.processing: Repeating backbone element for steps performed on the specimen before testing - description, procedure (e.g. centrifuged), time[x], and additive (Reference to a Substance/Medication used in processing).

Slide 3: container

Specimen.container: Describes the physical vessel - identifier, description, type (e.g. "Red top tube"), capacity, specimenQuantity, and additive[x] (e.g. EDTA anticoagulant already in the tube).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the split: collection = how it was taken, processing = what was done to it, container = what it was put in.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Study level

ImagingStudy represents a DICOM study. ImagingStudy.identifier typically carries the Study Instance UID. Other study-level fields: status, subject, started, numberOfSeries, numberOfInstances, procedureReference, basedOn (links to the ordering ServiceRequest).

Slide 2: Series level

ImagingStudy.series: Repeating backbone - uid (DICOM Series Instance UID), number, modality (coded, e.g. CT, MR, US), description, bodySite, laterality, numberOfInstances.

Slide 3: Instance level

series.instance: Repeating backbone - uid (DICOM SOP Instance UID), sopClass (Coding identifying the DICOM SOP Class), number, title.

Slide 4: Exam focus

The three-level nesting Study > Series > Instance maps directly to DICOM UIDs - a favorite exam mapping question.

Slide 1: ingredient

Medication.ingredient: Repeating backbone element. item[x] can be a CodeableConcept (e.g. an RxNorm ingredient code) or a Reference to a Substance/Medication.

isActive marks whether this is an active ingredient or an inactive excipient.

Slide 2: strength

ingredient.strength: A Ratio expressing the amount of ingredient per unit of medication, e.g. 500 mg / 1 tablet or 250 mg / 5 mL for a liquid.

Slide 3: form and amount

  • Medication.code - overall product code, often RxNorm

Slide 4: Exam focus

Slide 1: status

MedicationRequest.status: 1..1, required binding. Lifecycle values: active, on-hold, cancelled, completed, entered-in-error, stopped, draft, unknown.

statusReason (CodeableConcept) can explain why, e.g. "patient allergic."

Slide 2: intent

MedicationRequest.intent: 1..1, required binding. Values: proposal, plan, order, original-order, reflex-order, filler-order, instance-order, option.

Most prescriptions are intent order; a suggested-but-not-yet-authorized medication is proposal.

Slide 3: Why both are needed

  • status alone can't tell you if this was ever a real order vs a draft plan
  • intent alone can't tell you if an order is still active or was cancelled
  • Together they fully describe the request's current state and nature

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam trap: confusing status=draft (workflow state) with intent=plan (kind of request) - a request can be a draft order (intent=order, status=draft).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: substitution

MedicationRequest.substitution: Backbone element controlling pharmacy substitution. allowed[x] can be a boolean (simple yes/no) or a CodeableConcept (coded substitution type, e.g. "generic composition allowed").

substitution.reason explains why substitution is or isn't permitted, e.g. "formulary policy."

Slide 2: Why it matters

Prescribers may set allowed[x] = false to require the exact brand-name product be dispensed (e.g. for narrow therapeutic index drugs), overriding default generic-substitution rules.

Slide 3: reasonCode and reasonReference

  • reasonCode - coded clinical indication (e.g. "hypertension") for the prescription
  • reasonReference - Reference to the supporting Condition or Observation
  • These document why the medication was ordered, separate from substitution rules

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember substitution governs pharmacy dispensing choice; reasonCode/reasonReference governs clinical justification - don't mix the two purposes.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: performer structure

MedicationDispense.performer: Repeating backbone element with function (CodeableConcept) and actor (Reference).

actor can reference Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, Patient, Device, or RelatedPerson - covering automated dispensing devices too.

Slide 2: function values

  • dataenterer - entered the dispense information
  • packager - packaged the medication
  • checker - verified the dispense
  • finalchecker - pharmacist giving final verification before release

Slide 3: Multiple performers

A single dispense event can list several performers, each with a distinct function - reflecting real pharmacy workflow where different staff enter, fill, package, and check a prescription.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the function code set (dataenterer, packager, checker, finalchecker) and that actor is not limited to Practitioner - Device counts too.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: authorizingPrescription

MedicationDispense.authorizingPrescription: 0..*, Reference(MedicationRequest). Identifies the order(s) that authorize this dispense event.

Without this link, a dispense record would be disconnected from the prescriber's original order.

Slide 2: Partial fills

A single MedicationRequest can generate multiple MedicationDispense resources over time (e.g. a 90-day supply dispensed as three 30-day fills), each pointing back to the same authorizingPrescription.

Slide 3: Traceability chain

  • MedicationRequest - the order/prescription
  • MedicationDispense.authorizingPrescription - links back to that order
  • MedicationDispense.status - tracks preparation/in-progress/completed for this fill

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam scenario: tracing which order a given dispense fulfills always points to authorizingPrescription.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: MedicationAdministration

MedicationAdministration: Records that a dose was actually given to the patient - inpatient nursing administration, immunization clinics, infusion events. Includes performer, dosage, effective[x] (when given), and reasonCode.

Slide 2: MedicationStatement

MedicationStatement: A record of medication use that may come from the patient, a caregiver, or a chart review - not necessarily independently verified. Useful for medication reconciliation and history-taking.

status values include active, completed, intended, stopped, on-hold, not-taken, entered-in-error, unknown.

Slide 3: The four medication resources

  1. MedicationRequest - the order/prescription
  2. MedicationDispense - pharmacy fulfillment event
  3. MedicationAdministration - actual dose given, directly observed
  4. MedicationStatement - reported/summarized use, verification level varies

Slide 4: Exam focus

Choose based on certainty and source: a directly witnessed dose is MedicationAdministration; reported or reconciled history is MedicationStatement.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: vaccineCode

Immunization.vaccineCode: CodeableConcept identifying the vaccine product administered. In the US, commonly coded with CVX (CDC vaccine codes), sometimes alongside NDC.

Slide 2: lotNumber and manufacturer

Immunization.lotNumber: String recording the manufacturer's lot/batch number - critical for recall tracking and adverse event investigation.

Related fields: manufacturer (Reference(Organization)), expirationDate.

Slide 3: status

Immunization.status: Required binding - completed (given), entered-in-error, or not-done (vaccine was not administered).

When status is not-done, statusReason (CodeableConcept) should explain why, e.g. patient declined or a contraindication.

Slide 4: Exam focus

not-done is a real, valid status meaning the vaccination did not happen - conceptually paired with a statusReason.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: protocolApplied structure

Immunization.protocolApplied: Repeating backbone element describing which immunization protocol/schedule this dose follows.

Fields: series (name of the vaccination series), authority (Reference(Organization) defining the protocol), targetDisease (CodeableConcept, 0..*).

Slide 2: Dose numbering

doseNumber[x]: positiveInt or string - which dose in the series this administration represents (e.g. dose 2).

seriesDoses[x]: positiveInt or string - total number of doses needed to complete the series (e.g. 3).

Slide 3: Why it matters

  • Supports clinical decision support for "is this patient up to date?"
  • Multiple protocolApplied entries can exist if a dose counts toward more than one schedule/disease target
  • targetDisease lets one Immunization satisfy tracking for combination vaccines (e.g. MMR covers three diseases)

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember doseNumber[x] and seriesDoses[x] can be numeric or free-text string (e.g. "booster") - not strictly integers.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: reaction

Immunization.reaction: Repeating backbone element for adverse reactions following vaccination. Fields: date, detail (Reference to an Observation describing the reaction), and reported (boolean - was this patient-reported vs clinically observed).

Slide 2: programEligibility and fundingSource

Immunization.programEligibility: CodeableConcept indicating the patient's eligibility category for a vaccination program - in the US, commonly VFC (Vaccines for Children) eligibility codes.

Immunization.fundingSource: CodeableConcept distinguishing whether the dose was publicly or privately funded.

Slide 3: Related quality fields

  • isSubpotent (boolean) - flags a dose considered less than fully potent (e.g. after a cold-chain break)
  • subpotentReason (CodeableConcept) - explains why the dose is subpotent
  • These fields support revaccination decision-making

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know that reaction.detail points to an Observation (not inline reaction text), and that programEligibility/fundingSource are administrative, not clinical, fields on Immunization.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two roles, one policy

The Coverage resource separates the person who holds the policy from the person receiving care under it.

Coverage.subscriber - Reference(Patient|RelatedPerson) who owns the policy with the payer.

Coverage.beneficiary - Reference(Patient) who is entitled to the benefits (required).

Slide 2: Identifying the subscriber

  • Coverage.subscriberId - the member/subscriber ID assigned by the payer, used on claims and eligibility checks
  • Coverage.dependent - a string identifying the beneficiary as a dependent under the subscriber's policy

Slide 3: Relationship coding

Coverage.relationship is a CodeableConcept bound to the Subscriber Relationship Codes value set, with values such as self, spouse, child, parent, and other.

When beneficiary and subscriber are the same person, relationship is coded self.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect a scenario where the patient (beneficiary) is a child on a parent's (subscriber's) policy-know which element holds which Reference.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: The payer

Coverage.payor - one or more References (typically Organization) identifying who is financially responsible for reimbursing claims under this coverage.

Coverage.type - a CodeableConcept classifying the coverage itself, such as medical, dental, vision, or auto insurance.

Slide 2: Coverage.class structure

Each entry in Coverage.class is a BackboneElement with:

  • type - CodeableConcept naming the kind of class (group, plan, subgroup, subplan, class, subclass, sequence, rxbin, rxpcn, rxid, rxgroup)
  • value - the actual identifier string
  • name - human-readable display name for the class

Slide 3: Why it matters

Plan and group identifiers let payers route eligibility checks and claims to the correct benefit plan and employer group, and pharmacy-specific rx class values (bin/pcn/group/id) are required for pharmacy claims routing (NCPDP).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Do not confuse Coverage.payor (who pays) with Coverage.class (how the policy is categorized within that payer's book of business).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Coverage.period

Coverage.period is a Period element giving the start and (optionally open-ended) end date the policy is in force. Claims and eligibility checks should fall within this window.

Coverage.status tracks the record's lifecycle: active, cancelled, draft, or entered-in-error.

Slide 2: Coordination of benefits (COB)

When a patient has multiple Coverage resources, Coverage.order (a positiveInt) establishes the COB sequence: 1 = primary payer, 2 = secondary, 3 = tertiary, and so on. Claims are submitted to the primary first, then remainder billed to the secondary.

Slide 3: Network and cost sharing

  • Coverage.network - string identifying the provider network for this plan
  • Coverage.costToBeneficiary - BackboneElement listing copay, deductible, or coinsurance amounts/exceptions

Slide 4: Exam focus

A question describing a patient with two insurances is testing whether you know order=1 identifies the primary payer, not which Coverage was created first.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Purpose of the request

CoverageEligibilityRequest asks a payer whether a patient's coverage is active and what benefits apply. CoverageEligibilityRequest.purpose (repeating code) states why: auth-requirements, benefits, discovery, or validation.

Slide 2: The insurance block

CoverageEligibilityRequest.insurance is a BackboneElement with:

  • focal - boolean marking the coverage being evaluated in this request
  • coverage - Reference(Coverage)
  • businessArrangement - optional additional contract identifier

Slide 3: Requested services

CoverageEligibilityRequest.item lets the requester scope the check to specific services:

  • category - benefit category (e.g., medical care, vision, pharmacy)
  • productOrService - specific service/procedure code
  • provider, quantity, unitPrice, facility, diagnosis

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know that omitting item entirely produces a general eligibility/benefits response, while populating it requests benefit detail for those specific services.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Response outcome

CoverageEligibilityResponse.outcome summarizes processing: complete (fully processed), error (could not be processed), or partial (some information could not be returned).

insurance.inforce tells the requester whether the coverage was active on the servicedDate/servicedPeriod checked.

Slide 2: Benefit detail structure

Each insurance.item can carry one or more benefit entries:

  • type - CodeableConcept (e.g., copay, deductible, visits remaining)
  • allowed[x] - the total allowed amount, count, or description
  • used[x] - the amount already consumed

Slide 3: Other item flags

  • item.excluded - boolean, true if the service is not covered
  • item.authorizationRequired - boolean flagging prior authorization needs
  • item.category / item.productOrService - what the benefit detail applies to

Slide 4: Exam focus

A partial outcome with an error entry pointing to specific items is a common exam distractor-know that partial is not the same as error.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Claim.diagnosis

Each entry has a sequence (positiveInt), diagnosis[x] (CodeableConcept or Reference(Condition)), and a type CodeableConcept indicating role-e.g. admitting, principal, secondary. Institutional claims also use onAdmission and packageCode (e.g., DRG).

Slide 2: Claim.procedure

Each entry has a sequence, a date, and procedure[x] (CodeableConcept or Reference(Procedure)). A type can mark the primary procedure. udi references device identification when a device was used.

Slide 3: Claim.supportingInfo

A generic BackboneElement for anything else the payer needs: sequence, required category (CodeableConcept naming what kind of info this is, e.g. hospitalized, employmentImpacted, missingtooth), optional code, timing[x], and value[x] (many types allowed: boolean, string, Quantity, Attachment, Reference).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Line items reference these by number-item.diagnosisSequence, item.procedureSequence, and item.informationSequence-so a line item can point to exactly the diagnoses/procedures/info that justify it.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why list all insurance

A patient may have multiple coverages. Claim.insurance is repeating so the claim can declare all of them, letting downstream processors and secondary payers see what other coverage exists.

Slide 2: sequence and focal

  • sequence - positiveInt ordering the insurance list, typically matching COB order (1=primary)
  • focal - boolean; exactly one entry is true, identifying which coverage this claim submission is being adjudicated against right now

Slide 3: Supporting elements

  • coverage - Reference(Coverage)
  • businessArrangement - additional contract number
  • preAuthRef - prior authorization reference numbers
  • claimResponse - Reference to the ClaimResponse from a prior (e.g., primary) payer, used when billing a secondary payer

Slide 4: Exam focus

When re-submitting to a secondary payer after the primary adjudicates, a new Claim (or the same claim reprocessed) sets focal=true on the secondary's insurance entry and can reference the primary's ClaimResponse.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Adjudication categories

ClaimResponse.item.adjudication is repeating per line item, each with:

  • category - CodeableConcept such as submitted, eligible, deductible, copay, coinsurance, or benefit
  • reason - CodeableConcept explaining adjustments or denial
  • amount / value - the Money or decimal for that category

Slide 2: Totals

ClaimResponse.total summarizes adjudication categories across the whole claim (e.g., total submitted vs total benefit paid), mirroring the per-item categories at the claim level.

Slide 3: Errors

ClaimResponse.error flags processing problems using itemSequence, detailSequence, and subDetailSequence to point back at the exact Claim line, plus a code describing the issue (e.g., invalid code, missing required field).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish a business denial (adjudication.category=benefit with amount 0 and a denial reason) from a technical error entry meaning the claim/line could not even be adjudicated.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: EOB.total

ExplanationOfBenefit.total is repeating: each entry has a category (CodeableConcept, e.g. submitted, benefit) and an amount (Money), giving claim-wide financial summaries that mirror the adjudication categories used at the item level.

Slide 2: EOB.payment

EOB.payment describes the actual disbursement: type, adjustment (Money), adjustmentReason, date, amount, and identifier (e.g., a check or EFT trace number).

Slide 3: EOB.benefitBalance

Reports the patient's plan-level benefit status, independent of this single claim:

  • category - benefit category (medical, pharmacy, vision...)
  • network, unit (individual/family), term (annual/lifetime)
  • financial - type + allowed[x] (total available) + used[x] (consumed so far)

Slide 4: Exam focus

Do not confuse claim-specific total/payment with plan-wide benefitBalance, which reflects the member's overall remaining benefit, not this claim alone.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Provider and care team

EOB.provider - Reference(Practitioner|PractitionerRole|Organization), the billing provider for the claim.

EOB.careTeam is repeating, each entry with sequence, provider, responsible (boolean, lead provider), role, and qualification.

Slide 2: Diagnoses and procedures

EOB.diagnosis and EOB.procedure mirror the Claim resource's structures: each entry has a sequence, a coded or referenced value, and a type. These sequences let line items point back to the exact diagnosis/procedure that supports them.

Slide 3: Line items

EOB.item is the core billing line: sequence, careTeamSequence, diagnosisSequence, procedureSequence, productOrService, quantity, unitPrice, net, and its own adjudication results. Items can have nested detail and subDetail for further breakdown.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect a question asking which sequence array on item links to which top-level list (careTeam, diagnosis, or procedure)-know all three exist and are separate.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Conditional read

A client sends If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match (with an ETag) on a GET. If the resource has not changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth.

Slide 2: Conditional update

Instead of PUT to a known id, the client sends PUT [base]/Patient?identifier=.... The server searches:

  • 0 matches - server creates a new resource (like conditional create)
  • 1 match - server updates that resource
  • >1 match - server returns 412 Precondition Failed

Slide 3: Conditional delete

DELETE [base]/Patient?identifier=... deletes resource(s) matching the search. CapabilityStatement.rest.resource.conditionalDelete declares whether a server supports single or multiple conditional deletes.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know that conditional interactions rely on search parameters (update/delete) or cache headers (read)-not a resource id-which is what makes them useful when the client doesn't know the server-assigned id.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Conditional create

Client sends POST /Patient with header If-None-Exist: identifier=http://example.org/mrn|12345. The server runs that search first:

  • No match - creates the new resource normally (201 Created)
  • One match - returns the existing resource, no duplicate created
  • Multiple matches - server returns an error (412)

Slide 2: Conditional update

PUT /Patient?identifier=http://example.org/mrn|12345 with the resource body. This lets a client upsert a resource keyed by a business identifier rather than a FHIR id, useful for idempotent data loads.

Slide 3: Conditional delete

DELETE /Patient?identifier=http://example.org/mrn|12345 removes the matching resource(s). Servers advertise support via CapabilityStatement.rest.resource.conditionalDelete: not-supported, single (errors if >1 match), or multiple (deletes all matches).

Slide 4: Exam focus

A classic scenario: bulk-loading Patients from an external MRN without knowing FHIR ids-conditional create with If-None-Exist is the correct, idempotent technique.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: String and general modifiers

A modifier is appended to the parameter name with a colon: Patient?name:exact=Smith.

  • :exact - case- and accent-sensitive full string match
  • :contains - substring match anywhere in the value
  • :missing=true/false - works on almost any parameter to find resources where the element is absent or present

Slide 2: Token and reference modifiers

  • :text - matches the display text of a Coding/CodeableConcept rather than the code
  • :not - negates a token match
  • :above / :below - hierarchical code matching (e.g., broader/narrower SNOMED concepts)
  • :in / :not-in - membership test against a ValueSet
  • :identifier - search a reference parameter by a business identifier instead of a literal reference

Slide 3: Comparison prefixes

Prefixes go on the value, not the parameter name, and apply to number/date/quantity types: eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le, sa (starts after), eb (ends before), ap (approximately).

Example: Observation?date=ge2024-01-01&date=lt2024-02-01.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember modifiers change matching behavior and are type-restricted (e.g., :exact only applies to string parameters), while prefixes are for ordered types like date and number.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: _include and _revinclude

_include: MedicationRequest?_include=MedicationRequest:patient also returns the referenced Patient resources in the Bundle.

_revinclude: Patient?_revinclude=Observation:patient returns Observations that point back at the matched Patients. Both add entries with Bundle.entry.search.mode = include.

Slide 2: _sort and _count

_sort=birthdate sorts ascending; _sort=-birthdate sorts descending. Multiple comma-separated sort keys are allowed.

_count requests a page size (e.g., _count=20); it is a hint-servers may cap or ignore an excessive value, and pagination continues via Bundle.link relations (next/previous).

Slide 3: _summary and _elements

_summary: true (only summary elements), text (text, id, meta only), data (everything except text), count (just the total, no entries), false (full resources).

_elements=id,status,code restricts the returned elements to exactly that list. Both flag the resource with meta.tag SUBSETTED.

Slide 4: Exam focus

These parameters shape the response, not the match criteria-they never change which resources satisfy the search, only what's returned about them.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Validation and metadata

$validate - POST a resource (optionally with a profile parameter) to check conformance; returns an OperationOutcome without persisting anything.

$meta / $meta-add / $meta-delete - read or modify Resource.meta.tag, security, and profile independent of the resource content, avoiding a version bump for pure metadata changes.

Slide 2: $everything

GET /Patient/[id]/$everything returns a Bundle containing the Patient plus all directly and indirectly related resources (conditions, meds, observations, encounters, etc.), useful for record export or transfer-of-care. Encounter/[id]/$everything scopes similarly to one encounter.

Slide 3: Terminology operations

  • $expand (ValueSet) - returns the concrete list of codes in a value set
  • $lookup (CodeSystem) - returns details (display, properties, designations) for one code
  • $translate (ConceptMap) - maps a code from one system/value set to another
  • $document (Composition) - assembles a Bundle of type document from a Composition and its referenced resources

Slide 4: Exam focus

Operations are invoked with a leading $ on a type, instance, or the whole system-know which level each of these operations applies at.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why Parameters exists

Operations often need multiple named inputs or outputs that don't correspond to any single clinical resource. The Parameters resource provides a generic container for exactly that, without being persisted or searched like normal clinical data.

Slide 2: parameter structure

Each Parameters.parameter has:

  • name - string, required
  • value[x] - a primitive type (string, boolean, integer, code, etc.)
  • resource - a full FHIR resource, if the parameter's value is a resource
  • part - nested parameter entries, for grouped/complex values

Exactly one of value[x], resource, or part is typically used per parameter.

Slide 3: Where it's used

Operations like $validate (input: resource + optional profile/mode) and $expand (input: filters, count, offset) can take or return a Parameters instance when more than one input/output value is needed, instead of a bare resource body.

Slide 4: Exam focus

If an operation needs to send or receive more than one named value, expect the answer to involve wrapping them in a Parameters resource.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: document and message

document - the first entry must be a Composition; the Bundle represents a persistent, attested clinical document (like a discharge summary).

message - the first entry must be a MessageHeader; represents an event notification sent to trigger a workflow, following the FHIR messaging paradigm.

Slide 2: transaction and batch

transaction - a set of operations (each entry has request.method and request.url) processed as a single atomic unit; if any entry fails, the whole transaction rolls back. Internal references can use urn:uuid: placeholders resolved during processing.

batch - same entry shape as transaction, but each entry is processed independently; the server returns a batch-response Bundle with per-entry outcomes, and partial failure is allowed.

Slide 3: history, searchset, and collection

  • history - result of a _history interaction; entries represent versions of a resource over time, may include deleted versions
  • searchset - result of a search; includes Bundle.total, paging links (self/next/previous), and each entry's search.mode (match vs include)
  • collection - a plain grouping of resources with no special processing or ordering implied

Slide 4: Exam focus

If a scenario says "all changes must succeed together or none happen," the answer is transaction; if partial success is acceptable, it's batch.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Kicking off an export

Client sends GET [base]/$export (system-level), /Group/[id]/$export (all members of a Group), or /Patient/$export (all patients), with headers Accept: application/fhir+json and Prefer: respond-async.

Server responds 202 Accepted with a Content-Location header pointing to a status-polling endpoint.

Slide 2: Scoping the export

  • _type - comma-separated list of resource types to include
  • _since - only resources modified after this instant (incremental export)
  • _typeFilter - search-style filters narrowing specific resource types further

Slide 3: Polling and output

Client polls the status URL with GET. While processing, server returns 202 (optionally with an X-Progress header). When done, it returns 200 with a JSON manifest listing output entries: each has a type, a file url, and a count. Each file is NDJSON-one JSON resource per line, downloaded via a separate GET.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Bulk Data access typically pairs with SMART Backend Services (asymmetric JWT client-credential authorization) since no interactive user is present during the export.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: CapabilityStatement

CapabilityStatement: A resource a server publishes at /metadata describing what it supports - FHIR version, formats, security, and per-resource-type interactions (read, search, create, update, delete, history).

Clients query it to discover whether an interaction or search parameter is available before using it.

Slide 2: Key elements

  • fhirVersion - which FHIR release the server implements
  • rest.resource.interaction - supported CRUD/search operations per type
  • rest.resource.searchParam - which search parameters are supported
  • rest.operation - supported $operations

Slide 3: ImplementationGuide

ImplementationGuide: A resource that packages a coherent set of conformance artifacts - profiles, extensions, ValueSets, examples, and narrative pages - for a specific use case (e.g. US Core, Da Vinci).

global elements bind a resource type to a profile that applies IG-wide.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember: a CapabilityStatement answers "what can this server do?"; an ImplementationGuide answers "what are the rules for this use case?"

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Cardinality restriction

Profiling a resource can only make cardinality stricter than the base definition: 0..1 can become 1..1, and 0..* can become 0..5, but you can never loosen a base constraint (e.g. turn 0..1 into 0..2).

Slide 2: Fixed values

fixed[x]: Forces every instance conforming to the profile to carry this exact value for the element - all sub-elements must match precisely, with nothing extra and nothing missing.

Example: fixing Observation.code.coding.system to http://loinc.org.

Slide 3: Patterns

pattern[x]: Defines a required subset of content - the listed properties must be present and match, but the instance may include additional elements not mentioned in the pattern.

Common use: requiring a specific Coding (system+code) inside CodeableConcept.coding while still allowing other codings or text.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: fixed = exact match only; pattern = required subset, extra elements OK. Cardinality can only tighten, never loosen.

Slide 1: Where formats are declared

A server lists the representations it can produce and consume in CapabilityStatement.format, using short codes like json and xml, or full MIME types.

Slide 2: Standard media types

  • application/fhir+json - JSON representation (most common)
  • application/fhir+xml - XML representation
  • application/fhir+ndjson - newline-delimited JSON, used by Bulk Data $export

Slide 3: Content negotiation

Clients request a representation via the Accept HTTP header, or override it with the _format query parameter (e.g. ?_format=json) - useful when a client can't control headers directly.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Know that _format takes precedence for format selection even when Accept is also present, and that legacy application/json/application/xml are not the correct FHIR-specific media types.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: PDex - Payer Data Exchange

Da Vinci PDex: Lets a health plan expose a member's claims and clinical history (as US Core resources) so it follows them to a new payer or to a patient-facing app, using the Bulk Data Access $export operation.

Slide 2: CRD and DTR - the prior auth pipeline

  • CRD (Coverage Requirements Discovery): Uses CDS Hooks (order-select, order-sign) so the EHR asks the payer in real time whether an order needs prior authorization or has documentation requirements.
  • DTR (Documentation Templates and Rules): Launches a SMART app that renders a Questionnaire, runs CQL against the chart to auto-populate answers, and produces a QuestionnaireResponse.

Slide 3: PAS and beyond

PAS (Prior Authorization Support): Submits the completed request as a FHIR Claim using the $submit operation, receiving a ClaimResponse - a FHIR-native replacement for the X12 278 transaction.

Risk Adjustment / Gaps in Care and CDex (Clinical Data Exchange) round out the family: risk adjustment IGs report quality/HCC gaps, while CDex uses Task-based workflows for general payer-provider clinical data requests.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: CRD happens first (at ordering), DTR fills out the form, PAS submits it as a Claim - know that sequence.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Kicking off an export

$export is invoked at three levels: system (/$export, all data), Group (/Group/[id]/$export, an attributed patient population), or Patient (/Patient/$export or /Patient/[id]/$export).

The request must include Prefer: respond-async.

Slide 2: Async job pattern

The server immediately returns 202 Accepted with a Content-Location header pointing to a status endpoint.

The client polls that URL: 202 means still processing (optionally with an X-Progress header), 200 means done and returns a completion manifest.

Slide 3: Output and filters

The manifest lists download URLs for NDJSON files, one or more per resource type, fetched with Accept: application/fhir+ndjson.

  • _type - limit which resource types are exported
  • _since - only resources updated after a timestamp
  • _typeFilter - FHIR search-style filters per type

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Bulk Data is always asynchronous and returns NDJSON, never a synchronous Bundle - a scenario needing a large population export points to $export, not a plain search.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: system and version

Coding.system: A canonical URI that unambiguously identifies the code system (e.g. http://loinc.org, http://snomed.info/sct). Without it, a bare code is meaningless.

Coding.version: Optional - needed only when the meaning of a code could differ between versions of a system that changes over time.

Slide 2: display

Coding.display: The human-readable representation of the code's meaning, as defined by the code system - useful for UI rendering, but the system + code pair is what carries authoritative meaning, not the display text.

Slide 3: userSelected

Coding.userSelected: A boolean indicating this particular Coding is the one a person actually selected, when a CodeableConcept carries multiple Codings (e.g. original code plus a mapped/translated code).

Only one Coding in a given CodeableConcept should have userSelected = true.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: When a CodeableConcept has several Codings (e.g. local code + SNOMED translation), userSelected tells you which one the clinician actually chose.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: NamingSystem

NamingSystem: A resource that declares the identity of a code system, identifier system, or root - resolving informal identifiers (an OID, a UUID, or another URI) to the canonical URI FHIR expects.

kind is one of codesystem, identifier, or root; uniqueId lists the equivalent identifiers with their type.

Slide 2: Why it matters

Legacy systems often reference code systems by OID rather than URI. A NamingSystem lookup lets an implementer or tool translate 2.16.840.1.113883.6.1 into http://loinc.org, or resolve a local identifier system's assigning authority.

Slide 3: TerminologyCapabilities

TerminologyCapabilities: Describes what a terminology server supports - which code systems and value sets it knows, expansion parameters, and support for operations like $expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $translate, and $subsumes.

It is narrower and more specific than a general CapabilityStatement.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: NamingSystem is about identity/URIs; TerminologyCapabilities is about what terminology operations a server can perform.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What required means

Required binding: The strictest of the four binding strengths - a coded element's value SHALL come from the bound ValueSet. No other code is considered valid.

Slide 2: Where it's used

Applied to elements needing tight, closed interoperability, such as small internal FHIR code systems: AdministrativeGender (male/female/other/unknown), Address.use, ContactPoint.system.

Slide 3: Validation impact

A profile validator or terminology server will flag an instance as non-conformant if the coded value isn't in the required ValueSet - this is one of the few binding strengths that produces a hard validation error rather than a warning.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: "Required" = closed list, no exceptions; if a scenario code isn't in the ValueSet, the instance is invalid.

sections.summary: A required binding means every coded value in that element must come from the specified ValueSet - no other codes are conformant, making it the strictest of the four binding strengths.
sections.title: Required
sections.examTip: Required binding means the ValueSet is a hard membership rule; a code outside it fails validation.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What extensible means

Extensible binding: Implementers SHOULD use a code from the bound ValueSet if one exists that fits the concept being recorded. If the ValueSet genuinely has no matching concept, another code MAY be used instead.

Slide 2: Where it's used

Common on clinically variable CodeableConcept elements such as Condition.code or AllergyIntolerance.code, where a core value set covers common cases but real-world diagnoses can exceed it.

Slide 3: Compliance nuance

Using an outside code when a fitting ValueSet concept actually existed is considered a binding violation, even though extensible is more permissive than required - the escape hatch is only for genuine gaps.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Extensible = use the ValueSet unless it truly doesn't cover your concept; that's the key exam distinction from "required."

sections.title: Extensible
sections.examTip: Extensible only permits an outside code when no concept in the ValueSet fits - picking an outside code when a match exists is non-conformant.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What preferred means

Preferred binding: The bound ValueSet represents best practice and is encouraged, but implementers are free to use codes from any other system - there is no conformance penalty for deviating.

Slide 2: Purpose

Preferred bindings aim for consistency across implementations without forcing it, useful when a good default ValueSet exists but many valid clinical or business contexts fall outside it.

Slide 3: Validation impact

A validator will not flag an instance as invalid solely for using a code outside a preferred-bound ValueSet - at most it may generate an informational hint, never an error.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Preferred = suggestion, never enforced; don't confuse it with extensible's conditional requirement.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What example means

Example binding: The bound ValueSet is shown purely as an illustration of the kind of concept expected - it carries no conformance expectation whatsoever.

Slide 2: Where it's used

Used where the space of valid codes is too broad or domain-specific to usefully constrain, e.g. a generic CodeableConcept that could reasonably hold values from many different code systems depending on context.

Slide 3: Validation impact

A validator performs no meaningful check against an example-bound ValueSet - any code, from any system, or free text alone, is fully conformant.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Example = weakest strength, purely illustrative; never expect a validation error tied to an example binding.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: CPT

CPT (Current Procedural Terminology): Maintained by the American Medical Association, using 5-digit numeric codes to describe medical, surgical, and diagnostic procedures and professional services for billing.

CPT is proprietary and licensed - it generally cannot be freely redistributed in open packages.

Slide 2: HCPCS

HCPCS (Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System): Maintained by CMS, with two levels:

  • Level I - is CPT itself
  • Level II - alphanumeric codes (e.g. J-codes for drugs, E-codes for DME) covering supplies, equipment, and services CPT doesn't address

Slide 3: Where they appear in FHIR

Used as coding systems for Procedure.code, and heavily in billing/claims resources: Claim.item.productOrService, ExplanationOfBenefit, and Coverage-adjacent workflows like Da Vinci PAS.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: Distinguish CPT/HCPCS (procedures/billing) from ICD-10-CM (diagnoses) and SNOMED CT (general clinical concepts) - a claims scenario points to CPT/HCPCS.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What UCUM is

UCUM (Unified Code for Units of Measure): A code system providing precise, computable unit codes for use in Quantity data types across FHIR.

Quantity.system = http://unitsofmeasure.org; Quantity.code carries the UCUM code.

Slide 2: unit vs code

Quantity.unit: Human-readable display text (e.g. "milligrams").

Quantity.code: The machine-computable UCUM code (e.g. mg) used for calculation and comparison - this is what interoperable systems should rely on, not the free-text unit.

Slide 3: Case sensitivity

UCUM is strictly case sensitive: lowercase and uppercase letters represent different units or prefixes (e.g. g for gram vs. a capital-letter prefix meaning a different order of magnitude). Getting the case wrong silently changes the quantity's meaning.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Exam tip: UCUM's case sensitivity is a classic exam trap - always verify exact casing when validating a Quantity.code.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why auditability matters

Auditability is the ability to reconstruct who accessed or changed a resource, when, and under what authority-a core requirement for healthcare privacy and security regulations.

FHIR supports this through dedicated resources rather than a single audit field.

Slide 2: Core resources

  • AuditEvent - logs security-relevant events (read, create, login, export)
  • Provenance - records the who/what/when/why behind a resource's content
  • Resource.meta - versionId, lastUpdated, and security labels

Slide 3: Putting it together

A well-audited system logs an AuditEvent for every access, attaches Provenance to significant data changes, and preserves version history so any prior state of a resource can be reconstructed later.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the difference: AuditEvent = access/security log, Provenance = data lineage/attestation.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: AuditEvent purpose

AuditEvent records a security-relevant occurrence, such as a resource read, create, export, or a login attempt, for compliance and access-review purposes.

Slide 2: Key elements

  • type/subtype - category of event (e.g., RESTful, "read")
  • action - C/R/U/D/E (create, read, update, delete, execute)
  • recorded - instant the event was logged
  • outcome - 0=success, 4=minor failure, 8=serious, 12=major

Slide 3: Who and what

agent repeats to capture every actor involved (user, system, requestor) including their role and network address.

entity repeats to capture what was acted on-patient, resource instance, or a query string-plus optional entity.detail.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Match "who did it" to agent and "what was touched" to entity-a common exam confusion.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two separate checks

Input validation confirms a payload is structurally correct (cardinality, data types, terminology bindings). Authorization confirms the authenticated caller is allowed to perform that specific action on that specific resource or compartment.

Passing one does not imply passing the other.

Slide 2: Validation checklist

  • Reject required elements that are missing or mis-typed
  • Check code/Coding values against bound ValueSets
  • Enforce cardinality and invariants (e.g., FHIRPath constraints)
  • Never trust a client-supplied id or meta for security decisions

Slide 3: Authorization checklist

Confirm the token's SMART scopes (e.g., patient/*.read) cover the resource type and compartment requested, and that any patient-in-context restriction is enforced server-side, not merely trusted from the client.

Slide 4: Exam focus

A syntactically valid resource can still be an authorization failure-know both checks are required.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What makes an element a modifier

A modifier extension or modifier element changes the meaning of the data around it-for example, marking a diagnosis as "entered-in-error" or a procedure as "not-performed".

Unlike ordinary extensions, these cannot be safely ignored.

Slide 2: The safety rule

A receiving system must understand every modifierExtension it processes. If it does not recognize one, it must reject the resource rather than process it as if the modifier were absent.

Slide 3: Built-in modifier elements

  • Condition.verificationStatus = entered-in-error
  • Procedure.status = not-done, with statusReason
  • MedicationRequest.doNotPerform

These behave like modifiers even without using the modifierExtension mechanism.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Regular extensions can be ignored if unknown; modifierExtension can never be ignored.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Narrative and its risk

Every DomainResource can carry a text.div-human-readable HTML meant for display. Because it is HTML, an attacker could try to inject <script> tags or event handlers to run in a viewer's browser.

Slide 2: The allowed subset

  • Only a restricted XHTML subset is permitted (basic formatting, tables, lists)
  • No <script> tags, no inline event handlers (onclick, etc.)
  • No links to external resources (images, stylesheets)

Slide 3: Mitigation

Servers should validate or regenerate narrative on ingest rather than store client HTML verbatim, and viewers should render narrative through a sanitizing HTML renderer, never raw innerHTML without escaping.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Treat text.div like any untrusted HTML input-sanitize before storing or rendering.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Protecting the log itself

Audit records are only useful if they cannot be altered after the fact. Systems should make AuditEvent entries append-only and restrict update/delete on them far more tightly than on clinical data.

Slide 2: Access to logs

  • Only security/compliance roles should read AuditEvent broadly
  • Clinicians should not be able to alter their own access history
  • Export of audit data should itself be audited

Slide 3: Least privilege in practice

Every OAuth2 client and user account should request and receive the narrowest scope and patient compartment access it needs-avoid broad system/*.* grants when a narrower scope suffices.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Least privilege applies to both clinical data access and access to the audit trail itself.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why IGs add controls

Base FHIR R4 defines the mechanisms (AuditEvent, Consent, security labels) but leaves many policy decisions open. Implementation Guides close those gaps for a specific jurisdiction or use case.

Slide 2: Typical IG additions

  • Mandatory security labels on sensitive resource types
  • Required Consent checks before certain reads (e.g., 42 CFR Part 2 data)
  • Profiled AuditEvent with fixed type/subtype values

Slide 3: Checklist habit

Before certifying a build against an IG, read its dedicated Security and Privacy section-conformance to base R4 alone is not sufficient.

Slide 4: Exam focus

An IG's security rules are additive-they narrow or extend base R4, never relax its safety requirements.
