sections.detail:
Slide 1: Extension validation errors

The most common extension error is an Extension.url that does not match a known/registered definition-often a typo or a missing version segment in the canonical URL.

A profile validator (e.g., against US Core) will also flag missing Must Support extensions.

Slide 2: Extension vs modifierExtension

Using a regular extension when the content actually changes meaning (or the reverse) is a design error that validators cannot always catch, but reviewers should watch for it-it makes the resource unsafe to interpret correctly.

Slide 3: Narrative errors

  • text.div not well-formed XML/XHTML
  • Disallowed elements/attributes (script, style, external references)
  • text.status inconsistent with content (e.g., "generated" but empty)

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish a structural narrative error (bad XHTML) from a semantic extension error (wrong meaning, valid syntax).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: issue.severity

Every issue has a severity:

  • fatal - processing stopped entirely
  • error - the request could not be processed as submitted
  • warning - processed, but the caller should review something
  • information - purely informational note

Slide 2: issue.code

issue.code is bound to the required IssueType value set and categorizes the problem type independent of severity.

Slide 3: Common issue codes

  • required - missing mandatory element
  • value / invalid - bad content
  • invariant - failed constraint/FHIRPath rule
  • not-found, duplicate, security, not-supported

Slide 4: Exam focus

A warning or information issue can appear alongside a 200 OK-only error/fatal implies the request failed.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What diagnostics is for

issue.diagnostics holds a free-text explanation intended for a person reading the error-additional detail beyond the coded issue.code.

Slide 2: Diagnostics vs details

  • diagnostics - plain string, human-readable
  • details - CodeableConcept, can carry a coded application-specific reason plus text

Automated clients should key off code/details.coding, not parse diagnostics text.

Slide 3: Security consideration

Servers must avoid exposing sensitive internals-stack traces, database errors, file paths-through diagnostics, since it is often surfaced directly to API consumers.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Never design logic that parses diagnostics text to make a decision-it is unstructured by design.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Locating the problem

When a resource fails validation, the caller needs to know where, not just what. issue.expression and issue.location exist for exactly this.

Slide 2: expression vs location

  • expression - a FHIRPath (e.g., Patient.name[0].given) - the R4-preferred mechanism
  • location - an older XPath-like string, kept only for backward compatibility

Slide 3: Multiple paths

Both elements are repeating (0..*), so one issue can list several equivalent locations, such as an XML path and a JSON-oriented path pointing at the same data.

Slide 4: Exam focus

If asked which element to prefer in R4 for locating an error, choose expression over location.

Once headers are ruled out, inspect the actual request and response bodies-look for missing required elements, wrong data types, or an unexpected resource type in the response (often an OperationOutcome instead of the resource).

GET [base]/metadata returns a CapabilityStatement describing every resource type, interaction (read/search/update/etc.), and search parameter the server actually implements.

  • The interaction (e.g., patch) isn't implemented
  • The search parameter you're using isn't declared

Slide 4: Exam focus

Slide 1: Validate before you submit

Running a resource through a local validator-like the official validator_cli.jar or the IG Publisher-against base FHIR R4 and any relevant profile catches most problems before they ever reach the server.

  3. Repeat-later issues sometimes disappear once an earlier structural fault is fixed

Slide 4: Exam focus

Local, iterative validation is faster and safer than repeatedly guessing against a live server.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two layers of rules

An IG-conformant resource must satisfy both the base R4 specification and any applicable profile (a StructureDefinition that constrains the base further).

Slide 2: Isolating the layer

  1. Validate against base R4 only
  2. Validate against the profile
  3. Compare-issues appearing only in step 2 are profile-specific

Slide 3: Typical profile-only causes

  • Missing Must Support element
  • Failed slicing discriminator match
  • Tighter cardinality or binding strength
  • Extra FHIRPath invariant defined by the IG

Slide 4: Exam focus

"Passes base, fails profile" points straight at IG-specific constraints, not a malformed resource.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Verify terminology first

Coded-element failures should be checked against the actual ValueSet binding using the $validate-code operation, since a code can be well-formed JSON but still invalid for that binding.

Slide 2: Binding strength matters

  • required - mismatch is an error
  • extensible - error only if no reasonable code exists in the set
  • preferred/example - mismatch is at most a warning

Slide 3: Minimal payload retest

Strip the resource to the smallest set of required elements that still validates, then add optional/complex elements back one at a time until the failure reappears-this isolates the exact cause.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Don't assume your code is wrong-confirm the terminology server actually has that CodeSystem/ValueSet loaded.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why three case types?

Conformance testing checks that a server or client implementation actually enforces the rules declared in its CapabilityStatement and profiles.

Test suites are built from three complementary case types so that both correct and incorrect behavior get exercised, not just the happy path.

Slide 2: Positive and negative cases

  • Positive case - a fully conformant resource or request that must succeed (e.g., a valid Patient with all required elements)
  • Negative case - a resource that violates a rule (missing required element, wrong binding, bad reference) and must be rejected with an OperationOutcome

Slide 3: Boundary cases

Boundary cases sit at the edge of what is allowed:

  • Minimum and maximum cardinality (e.g., exactly 0 vs 1 occurrences)
  • String length limits and numeric ranges
  • Optional Must Support elements present vs absent

Tools like Touchstone and Inferno automate running these suites against R4 endpoints.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Expect questions asking you to classify a given test scenario as positive, negative, or boundary-know that a rejected, invalid example is negative, not a "failing boundary."

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Terminology testing

Terminology tests confirm that coded elements (code, Coding, CodeableConcept) actually conform to their declared binding strength and ValueSet.

These go beyond structural validation-a resource can be schema-valid yet still carry a code that isn't in the required ValueSet.

Slide 2: Key terminology operations

  • $validate-code - checks whether a code is a member of a ValueSet or CodeSystem
  • $expand - returns the concrete list of codes a ValueSet contains
  • $lookup - returns properties and designations for a single code
  • $translate - maps a code between two systems using a ConceptMap

Slide 3: Interoperability testing

Interoperability tests confirm that independently built systems can exchange FHIR data and interpret it the same way-covering things like matching identifier systems, consistent date/time handling, and shared terminology.

Connectathons are the classic HL7 venue for this kind of cross-vendor testing.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Distinguish structural validation (does the JSON/XML match the schema) from terminology testing (are the codes actually valid members of the bound ValueSet).

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Where it fits

Use-case definition is the starting phase of the implementation lifecycle: before any resource, profile, or endpoint is designed, the team documents what problem is being solved.

It answers who the actors are, what workflow is being supported, and what data must move between systems.

Slide 2: What gets documented

  • Actors - the systems and roles involved (e.g., EHR, lab system, patient app)
  • Workflow/process - the sequence of real-world events being digitized
  • Data requirements - which clinical or administrative data elements must be exchanged
  • Whether an existing Implementation Guide (e.g., US Core) already covers the use case

Slide 3: Downstream impact

A clear use case drives every later decision: which resources to profile, which elements are Must Support, and which RESTful interactions the CapabilityStatement needs to declare.

A vague or overly broad use case is a common root cause of implementation projects that stall in profiling.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the lifecycle ordering: use-case definition precedes capability/API design, security/validation, and deployment.

• Actors - the systems and roles involved (e.g., EHR, lab system, patient app)
  • Workflow/process - the sequence of real-world events being digitized
  • Data requirements - which clinical or administrative data elements must be exchanged
  • Whether an existing Implementation Guide (e.g., US Core) already covers the use case

slides.title: Downstream impact
slides.body:
A clear use case drives every later decision: which resources to profile, which elements are Must Support, and which RESTful interactions the CapabilityStatement needs to declare.

A vague or overly broad use case is a common root cause of implementation projects that stall in profiling.

slides.title: Exam focus
slides.body: Know the lifecycle ordering: use-case definition precedes capability/API design, security/validation, and deployment.

keyPoints: Identify actors (systems and roles) and the clinical or administrative workflow being supported
Document required data elements and existing standards or IGs that already cover the use case
Feeds directly into profiling decisions and the CapabilityStatement scope
Poorly scoped use cases lead to over-broad profiles and unusable Must Support lists

sections.detail:
Slide 1: From use case to API

Once a use case is defined, capability and API design decides how it will actually be exposed over FHIR's RESTful API-which resources, which interactions, and which operations.

Slide 2: CapabilityStatement

The CapabilityStatement resource is the formal, machine-readable declaration of what a server (or the requirements of a client) supports:

  • Supported resource types and profiles
  • Supported interactions - read, vread, update, patch, create, delete, search, history
  • Supported search parameters per resource

Slide 3: Custom operations

When standard REST interactions aren't enough, an OperationDefinition documents a custom $operation (e.g., $everything, $match) including its parameters and return type.

Prefer standard interactions and search parameters before adding custom operations.

Slide 4: Exam focus

A server's declared CapabilityStatement must accurately reflect what it actually implements-mismatches are a classic conformance failure.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Securing the API

Security in a FHIR implementation is layered on top of the REST API, most commonly via SMART on FHIR, which uses OAuth2 authorization-code or client-credentials flows plus scoped access tokens.

Slide 2: Scopes and consent

  • SMART scopes follow the pattern patient/Observation.read or user/*.write
  • Consent resources can express patient-directed data-sharing restrictions
  • AuditEvent and Provenance record who accessed or changed what, and when

Slide 3: Validation and testing

Before go-live, resources and transactions are checked against StructureDefinitions and profiles using a validator, and both positive and negative test cases are run to confirm the implementation rejects bad data and accepts good data.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Remember: FHIR defines the resources and REST API; SMART on FHIR is the separate, standard layer that adds OAuth2-based authorization.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Going live

Deployment moves a tested implementation into production: publishing the real endpoint, finalizing environment and security configuration, and confirming the live CapabilityStatement matches what was tested.

Slide 2: Monitoring

  • AuditEvent resources and server logs track access and changes
  • Operational metrics - uptime, latency, error rates on OperationOutcome
  • Ongoing conformance checks to catch drift between declared and actual behavior

Slide 3: Version migration

FHIR has released several major versions (DSTU2, STU3, R4, R4B, R5) with breaking structural changes between them.

Migrating requires explicit mapping of changed elements or resources-there is no automatic backward compatibility, so servers often support one primary version and negotiate it via the endpoint or fhirVersion.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Do not assume a resource valid in one FHIR version is automatically valid in another-version migration is a deliberate, mapped process.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why this step

Every FHIR interaction starts from a resource that actually parses. This step is about producing the smallest defensible Patient resource - not the richest one - so you have a clean baseline to build on in later steps.

Slide 2: Minimal Patient JSON

A valid starting point:

{
  "resourceType": "Patient",
  "name": [{ "family": "Alvarez", "given": ["Rosa"] }],
  "gender": "female",
  "birthDate": "1988-04-12"
}

No id is sent on create - the server assigns it.

Slide 3: Create via HTTP POST

POST [base]/Patient
Content-Type: application/fhir+json
Accept: application/fhir+json

{ ...Patient body... }

A successful create returns 201 Created with a Location header containing the new Patient/[id]/_history/1.

Slide 4: Exam focus

What good looks like: a 201 response and a server-assigned id - not a 400 because of a malformed date or a misspelled element name.

Slide 1: What's changing

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why validate now

You've built up a realistic Patient. Before treating it as 'done', run it through the validator the same way an exam scenario or a receiving server would.

Slide 2: Calling $validate

POST [base]/Patient/$validate
Content-Type: application/fhir+json

{ "resourceType": "Patient", ... }

Slide 3: Reading the OperationOutcome

{
  "resourceType": "OperationOutcome",
  "issue": [{
    "severity": "error",
    "code": "invalid",
    "diagnostics": "birthDate is not a valid date",
    "expression": ["Patient.birthDate"]
  }]
}

The expression tells you exactly which path to fix.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Practice reading issue.expression first - it's the fastest way to locate the broken element without re-reading the whole resource.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: The scenario

This lab builds a small, realistic clinical graph: a patient is seen by a practitioner at an organization, during an encounter, resulting in a diagnosed condition and a recorded observation.

Slide 2: Encounter shape

{
  "resourceType": "Encounter",
  "status": "finished",
  "class": {
    "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode",
    "code": "AMB"
  }
}

Slide 3: Condition and Observation

{
  "resourceType": "Condition",
  "code": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://snomed.info/sct", "code": "38341003", "display": "Hypertension" }] }
}

Create each resource on its own first - references come next.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Choosing the wrong resource type for a concept (e.g. putting a diagnosis in Observation) is a classic exam trap - match the resource to the real-world concept.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why linking matters

Six unconnected resources aren't a clinical record - the references are what turn them into a coherent story a system can query and reconstruct.

Slide 2: Subject references

"subject": { "reference": "Patient/48213" },
"encounter": { "reference": "Encounter/9001" }

Every clinical resource in this lab should carry both a subject and an encounter reference.

Slide 3: Using urn:uuid before create

"subject": { "reference": "urn:uuid:3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6" }

Use this form when the referenced resource doesn't have a server id yet - it will map to a fullUrl in the transaction Bundle in the next step.

Slide 4: Exam focus

A reference that points to a resource of the wrong type or a nonexistent id fails validation even if the JSON is otherwise perfect.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why a transaction

Submitting six resources one at a time risks a partial write if something fails midway. A transaction Bundle is all-or-nothing: either every resource is created, or none are.

Slide 2: Bundle entry shape

{
  "fullUrl": "urn:uuid:3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6",
  "resource": { "resourceType": "Patient", ... },
  "request": { "method": "POST", "url": "Patient" }
}

Slide 3: Submitting the Bundle

POST [base]
Content-Type: application/fhir+json

{
  "resourceType": "Bundle",
  "type": "transaction",
  "entry": [ ... six entries ... ]
}

Slide 4: Exam focus

Mixing up batch and transaction semantics - or forgetting request.method on an entry - is the most common reason a submitted Bundle is rejected.

slides.body:

Content-Type: application/fhir+json

  "resourceType": "Bundle",
  "type": "transaction",
  "entry": [ ... six entries ... ]
}

keyPoints: Bundle.type must be "transaction" (not "batch", which has no atomicity guarantee)
Each entry needs fullUrl, resource, and request.method/url
Use POST for creates; use PUT for conditional updates or fixed ids
The server returns a 200 response Bundle with one entry.response per submitted entry, in order
sections.summary: Package all six linked resources into a single atomic transaction Bundle so they are created together, with references resolved via fullUrl instead of pre-existing server ids.
sections.title: Submit a transaction Bundle
sections.examTip: In a transaction Bundle, entry.fullUrl (a urn:uuid) is what lets references between not-yet-created resources resolve correctly on the server.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Search basics

Search is how real clients find resources without knowing ids in advance. This step exercises the two most common filters: a business identifier and a date range.

Slide 2: Searching by identifier

GET [base]/Patient?identifier=http://hospital.example.org/mrn|MRN-48213

Omitting the system (identifier=MRN-48213) matches on value alone across any system.

Slide 3: Searching by date

GET [base]/Encounter?date=ge2024-01-01&date=le2024-12-31

Repeating a parameter narrows the range; a bare date=2024-06-01 matches that day.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the date prefixes cold - eq, ge, le, gt, lt - the exam frequently tests which prefix produces an inclusive vs exclusive boundary.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Beyond simple filters

Real queries often need to filter by a related resource, and also want that related resource returned so the client doesn't need a second round trip.

Slide 2: Chained search

GET [base]/Observation?subject:Patient.name=Alvarez

Reads as: find Observations whose subject is a Patient whose name matches 'Alvarez'.

Slide 3: Adding _include

GET [base]/Observation?code=8480-6&_include=Observation:subject

The response Bundle now contains the Observations (match) plus the referenced Patients (include).

Slide 4: Exam focus

Don't confuse the search-mode outcome: chaining filters results, _include only adds extra resources - it never removes anything the base query matched.

slides.title: Beyond simple filters
slides.body: Real queries often need to filter by a related resource, and also want that related resource returned so the client doesn't need a second round trip.

slides.title: Chained search
slides.body:
GET [base]/Observation?subject:Patient.name=Alvarez

Reads as: find Observations whose subject is a Patient whose name matches 'Alvarez'.

slides.title: Adding _include
slides.body:
GET [base]/Observation?code=8480-6&_include=Observation:subject

The response Bundle now contains the Observations (match) plus the referenced Patients (include).

slides.title: Exam focus
slides.body: Don't confuse the search-mode outcome: chaining filters results, _include only adds extra resources - it never removes anything the base query matched.

keyPoints: Chained search syntax: param:TargetType.targetParam=value
_include=Observation:subject brings the referenced Patient into the same Bundle
_revinclude works the other direction: find Patients and pull in resources that reference them
Chaining and including are independent features and can be combined in one query
sections.summary: Search Observations by a property of the referenced Patient using chained search syntax, and use _include to pull the referenced Patient back in the same response.
sections.title: Use chained search and _include
sections.examTip: Chained search (Observation?subject:Patient.name=Smith) filters by a related resource's attribute; _include just adds already-matched related resources to the results without filtering by them.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why this matters

Knowing how to correctly read a search response Bundle is as important as writing the search query - misreading it leads to wrong conclusions about what actually matched.

Slide 2: Bundle shape

{
  "resourceType": "Bundle",
  "type": "searchset",
  "total": 2,
  "link": [{ "relation": "self", "url": "..." }],
  "entry": [ ... ]
}

Slide 3: Reading entry.search.mode

{
  "fullUrl": ".../Observation/501",
  "resource": { "resourceType": "Observation", ... },
  "search": { "mode": "match" }
}

An entry from _include shows "mode": "include" instead.

Slide 4: Exam focus

If asked how many resources actually matched the query, count entries with search.mode = match - not the total entry count, which may include extra resources.

sections.summary: Read the anatomy of the searchset Bundle returned by the previous queries: Bundle.type, total, entry.search.mode, and the paging links.
sections.title: Interpret a searchset Bundle
sections.examTip: entry.search.mode distinguishes resources that satisfied the query ("match") from resources only present because of _include ("include").

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why compare

Before you can conform to a profile, you need to see precisely how it differs from the base resource - that's what the differential is for.

Slide 2: Base vs constrained

// Base Patient: identifier is 0..*, optional
// US Core Patient profile differential:
{
  "path": "Patient.identifier",
  "min": 1,
  "max": "*"
}

The profile makes at least one identifier required.

Slide 3: Fetching the StructureDefinition

GET [base]/StructureDefinition?url=http://hl7.org/fhir/us/core/StructureDefinition/us-core-patient

Slide 4: Exam focus

Profiles constrain, they never loosen the base spec - if a differential appears to widen cardinality, re-check which direction min/max moved.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two separate signals

Must Support and terminology binding strength are often taught together but answer different questions: 'must the system handle this element?' vs 'how strictly must its codes match a ValueSet?'

Slide 2: Spotting Must Support

{
  "path": "Patient.identifier",
  "mustSupport": true
}

Scan the differential for mustSupport: true flags element by element.

Slide 3: Spotting binding strength

{
  "path": "Patient.gender",
  "binding": {
    "strength": "required",
    "valueSet": "http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/administrative-gender"
  }
}

Slide 4: Exam focus

Memorize the binding strength ladder: required > extensible > preferred > example, from strictest to loosest.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: From generic to profile-specific

Lab 1 validated against the base spec. This step raises the bar: validating against the actual US Core profile the resource is claimed to conform to.

Slide 2: Validating against a profile

POST [base]/Patient/$validate?profile=http://hl7.org/fhir/us/core/StructureDefinition/us-core-patient

{ "resourceType": "Patient", ... }

Slide 3: A typical profile error

{
  "severity": "error",
  "diagnostics": "Patient.identifier: minimum required = 1, but only found 0",
  "expression": ["Patient"]
}

Add the missing identifier and re-submit.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Declaring meta.profile on a resource that doesn't actually satisfy the profile's constraints is a conformance failure the exam likes to test.

Missing Must Support elements may surface as warnings depending on the validator
Re-run $validate after every fix - do not batch corrections blind

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why expand

A ValueSet's compose rules describe how to build its members, but clients usually just want the resulting flat list - that's what $expand hands back.

Slide 2: Calling $expand

GET [base]/ValueSet/$expand?url=http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/administrative-gender

Slide 3: Reading the expansion

{
  "resourceType": "ValueSet",
  "expansion": {
    "contains": [
      { "system": "http://hl7.org/fhir/administrative-gender", "code": "male" },
      { "system": "http://hl7.org/fhir/administrative-gender", "code": "female" }
    ]
  }
}

Slide 4: Exam focus

$expand answers 'what codes are in this set' - it does not check whether a specific code is valid; that's $validate-code, the next step.

compose.include can pull codes from a whole CodeSystem or filter by concept/filter rules
Large ValueSets may return a partial expansion with paging via offset/count parameters
The expansion reflects the terminology server's current content - it can change over time
sections.summary: Call the $expand operation on a ValueSet to retrieve its full list of member codes, and understand how compose.include rules determine what gets expanded.
sections.title: Expand a ValueSet
sections.examTip: $expand can be called on a ValueSet by canonical url or by POSTing the ValueSet body directly - both are legal.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two related operations

Now that you can expand a full ValueSet, the next question is per-code: is this specific code valid here, and what does it actually mean?

Slide 2: Validating a code

GET [base]/ValueSet/$validate-code?url=http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/administrative-gender&system=http://hl7.org/fhir/administrative-gender&code=female

Returns { "name": "result", "valueBoolean": true } in a Parameters resource.

Slide 3: Looking up a code

GET [base]/CodeSystem/$lookup?system=http://loinc.org&code=8480-6

Returns the code's display ("Systolic blood pressure") and any defined properties.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Don't confuse the two: $validate-code = is it in this set, $lookup = what does it mean.

The response is a Parameters resource with a boolean "result" and optional "message"
$lookup is called on CodeSystem and returns display, definition, and designations
Use $lookup to resolve a display string when your data only has a bare code

sections.examTip: $validate-code checks membership in a ValueSet (or CodeSystem); $lookup answers a different question - what does this code mean and what properties does it carry.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why translation matters

Different systems standardize on different code systems. $translate bridges them using a curated ConceptMap instead of ad hoc lookup tables.

Slide 2: Calling $translate

GET [base]/ConceptMap/$translate?url=http://example.org/fhir/ConceptMap/local-to-snomed&system=http://example.org/local-codes&code=BP-SYS

Slide 3: Reading the result

{
  "parameter": [
    { "name": "result", "valueBoolean": true },
    { "name": "match", "part": [
      { "name": "equivalence", "valueCode": "equivalent" },
      { "name": "concept", "valueCoding": { "system": "http://snomed.info/sct", "code": "271649006" } }
    ]}
  ]
}

Slide 4: Exam focus

Know the equivalence vocabulary - equivalent, wider, narrower, inexact - an exact code match is not guaranteed just because a mapping exists.

Input parameters are system, code, and the target (or source) system
The response lists match.equivalence and match.concept for each candidate mapping
Not every code has an exact equivalent - equivalence conveys how close the match is
sections.summary: Use the $translate operation with a ConceptMap to convert a code from one terminology system to an equivalent code in another (e.g. a local code to SNOMED CT).
sections.title: Translate between systems
sections.examTip: $translate returns one or more matches with an equivalence value (equivalent, wider, narrower, inexact, etc.) - not always a single exact answer.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why discovery first

Before an app can authenticate, it needs to know where to send the user and where to exchange codes for tokens - both are published, not assumed.

Slide 2: SMART configuration

GET [base]/.well-known/smart-configuration
{
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://auth.example.org/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://auth.example.org/token",
  "capabilities": ["launch-standalone", "client-public"]
}

Slide 3: CapabilityStatement

GET [base]/metadata

Confirms which resource types and interactions (read/search/create) the server actually supports before you build against it.

Slide 4: Exam focus

A client that skips discovery and hardcodes auth URLs breaks the moment it points at a different FHIR server - discovery is what makes SMART apps portable.

Discovery should happen before any token request, not after a failed call
Endpoint URLs can differ per environment (sandbox vs production) - never hardcode across environments

sections.examTip: SMART discovery is always the first step of any app launch - never hardcode auth endpoints when a conformant server publishes them.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: The flow so far

With endpoints discovered in the previous step, this step actually runs the OAuth2 authorization code flow to obtain a usable access token.

Slide 2: Authorization request

GET https://auth.example.org/authorize?
  response_type=code&
  client_id=abc123&
  redirect_uri=https://app.example.org/callback&
  scope=patient/Observation.read launch/patient&
  state=xyz

Slide 3: Exchanging the code for a token

POST https://auth.example.org/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=abc&redirect_uri=...
{ "access_token": "...", "expires_in": 3600, "patient": "48213" }

Slide 4: Exam focus

Requesting overly broad scopes (e.g. system/*.* for a patient-facing app) is a security smell the exam expects you to flag.

The token response includes access_token, expires_in, and often a patient context parameter

sections.title: Request scopes and token
sections.examTip: SMART scopes follow the pattern [context]/[Resource].[permission], e.g. patient/Observation.read - always request the narrowest scope that satisfies the use case.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Using the token

With a token in hand, this step makes a real protected call - and then studies what the server says when that call is rejected.

Slide 2: Authenticated request

GET [base]/Observation?patient=48213
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

Slide 3: Reading a failure response

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"

{ "resourceType": "OperationOutcome", "issue": [{ "severity": "error", "code": "forbidden" }] }

Slide 4: Exam focus

401 vs 403 is a favorite exam distinction: 401 = who are you, 403 = I know who you are, but no.

keyPoints: Send the token as Authorization: Bearer [access_token]
401 Unauthorized: token missing, expired, or malformed - re-authenticate
403 Forbidden: token is valid but lacks the required scope - request a broader scope, don't just retry
WWW-Authenticate response headers often name the specific problem
sections.summary: Use the access token to call a protected FHIR endpoint, then deliberately trigger and correctly interpret both a 401 (no/invalid token) and a 403 (valid token, insufficient scope) response.

sections.examTip: 401 means authentication failed (bad or missing token); 403 means authentication succeeded but authorization was denied (token lacks the needed scope) - the fix for each is different.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: The scenario

You're handed a transaction Bundle that a colleague says 'doesn't work.' Before fixing anything, build a complete list of what's actually broken.

Slide 2: A broken entry example

{
  "fullUrl": "urn:uuid:aaa-111",
  "resource": { "resourceType": "Observation", "subject": { "reference": "urn:uuid:bbb-222" } },
  "request": { "method": "GET", "url": "Observation" }
}

Two problems here: the method is wrong for a create, and bbb-222 may not exist anywhere else in the Bundle.

Slide 3: Building your issue list

Walk every entry and note: (1) mismatched or missing fullUrl, (2) wrong request.method, (3) references to a urn:uuid that no entry defines.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Resist fixing as you go on your first pass - a full inventory of defects prevents you from 'fixing' a symptom while missing the actual root cause.

keyPoints: Check that every fullUrl is unique and actually referenced somewhere if it's a urn:uuid
Check that request.method matches the intent (POST for create, PUT for update)
Check that every reference.reference resolves to an entry's fullUrl or a real server id
List every issue found before making any edits
sections.summary: Given a deliberately broken transaction Bundle, systematically inspect every entry's fullUrl, resource content, and request block to catalog what's wrong before touching anything.
sections.title: Inspect a Bundle
sections.examTip: Diagnose fully before fixing - a Bundle can have more than one independent defect, and fixing the first one you spot can mask the others.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Fixing the reference

Correct the mismatched uuid so the Observation's subject reference matches the Patient entry's fullUrl exactly.

Slide 2: Before and after

// broken
"subject": { "reference": "urn:uuid:bbb-222" }

// fixed - matches the Patient entry's fullUrl
"subject": { "reference": "urn:uuid:aaa-111" }

Slide 3: Fixing the method

// broken
"request": { "method": "GET", "url": "Observation" }

// fixed
"request": { "method": "POST", "url": "Observation" }

Slide 4: Exam focus

A reference that resolves within the Bundle but a request.method that's still wrong will still fail the transaction - fix both categories, not just the one you found first.

Use POST + a resource-type-only url (e.g. "Patient") for creates
Use PUT + "ResourceType/id" for updates to a known resource
Fix one category of defect at a time, then re-inspect before moving to the next
sections.summary: Correct each defect found in the previous step: align fullUrl values with the references that point to them, and set the correct HTTP method on each entry's request block.
sections.title: Repair references and methods
sections.examTip: Every urn:uuid used in a reference must exactly match an entry's fullUrl elsewhere in the same Bundle - a typo or mismatched case breaks resolution.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Closing the loop

This is the last mile of Lab 7: submit, read the failure precisely, fix, and resubmit until the transaction succeeds cleanly.

Slide 2: A transaction failure

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

{
  "resourceType": "OperationOutcome",

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What recall questions test

Recall questions are the simplest topic-quiz format: they ask you to state a fact directly from the FHIR R4 specification, with no scenario to work through.

Slide 2: Typical examples

  • "What is the cardinality of Patient.identifier?"
  • "Which resource represents a lab result?"
  • "What binding strength allows codes outside the ValueSet when necessary?"

Slide 3: How to prepare

Recall questions reward direct familiarity with resource definitions, base cardinalities, and core value sets.

Reviewing the R4 resource index and data type pages is more effective prep here than scenario practice.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Do not overthink a recall item-if you know the fact, answer it directly rather than searching for a hidden scenario.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why this format exists

Scenario and specification-navigation questions test a different skill than recall: given a realistic situation, can you find the correct answer by navigating the FHIR R4 specification itself?

Slide 2: How it plays out

A question might describe an interoperability requirement (e.g., "a lab wants to report a new panel result") and ask which resource, element, or search parameter satisfies it-mirroring the real-world task of opening hl7.org/fhir and finding the right page.

Slide 3: Preparing effectively

  • Practice using the FHIR spec's resource index and search
  • Know which resource family covers a workflow (e.g., Observation for results, ServiceRequest for orders)
  • Get comfortable jumping between a resource page and its referenced definitions

Slide 4: Exam focus

Speed at locating the right spec page under time pressure matters as much as raw knowledge for this question type.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What you're given

Payload interpretation questions show you an actual FHIR R4 JSON (or XML) resource instance-often a Bundle, Patient, or Observation-and ask what a specific field means or contains.

Slide 2: Skills tested

  • Correctly reading a value[x] polymorphic element (e.g., valueQuantity vs valueCodeableConcept)
  • Tracing a reference string to the resource it points to
  • Reading nested Coding.system and Coding.code pairs correctly
  • Interpreting Bundle.entry structure in a searchset or transaction

Slide 3: Common traps

A frequent trap is misattributing a code to the wrong system when a CodeableConcept carries multiple Codings, or missing that a reference uses a contained or local id.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Slow down and read the payload field-by-field; these questions test careful reading, not deep spec recall.

Slide 1: Two related skills

This category blends two skills: debugging a broken FHIR resource or interaction, and resource selection-picking the right resource type for a scenario.

Slide 2: Debugging patterns

  • Read the OperationOutcome.issue list: severity, code, and diagnostics
  • Check for missing required elements, invalid codes, or unresolved reference targets
  • Watch for cardinality violations (e.g., a 0..1 element repeated)

Slide 3: Resource selection

Choosing between similar resources is a frequent exam pattern: Condition (diagnosis or problem) vs Observation (a measured or assessed finding) vs AllergyIntolerance (a specific safety-relevant risk).

Match the resource to its defined scope of use, not just its name.

Slide 4: Exam focus

For debugging items, let the OperationOutcome details drive your answer instead of guessing from the resource alone.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What blueprint weighting means

The certification exam has an official blueprint that assigns each content domain a percentage of the total exam (e.g., resources/data types, RESTful API, terminology, security).

Domain assessments are built to mirror those same percentages.

Slide 2: Why it matters

  • A domain worth 25% of the blueprint gets roughly 25% of assessment questions
  • This keeps your practice score's composition realistic, not artificially even across topics
  • Weak performance in a heavily-weighted domain has outsized impact on your real exam score

Slide 3: Using it to study

Check your per-domain score, not just the overall percentage-a strong overall score can hide a weak result in a high-weight domain.

Direct extra review time toward domains that are both low-scoring and high-weight.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Blueprint weighting is published by the certifying body and can change between exam versions-always check the current version before final review.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What it simulates

Timed randomized exams reproduce real certification-exam conditions: a fixed time limit and a question set drawn at random from the full bank rather than a fixed, memorizable sequence.

Slide 2: Randomization details

  • Question selection is randomized per attempt, within the domain-weighting rules
  • Answer-option order is typically shuffled too, preventing position-based guessing
  • Retaking the mock exam gives a different question mix, not a repeat

Slide 3: Why pacing matters

The timer forces the same pacing discipline required on exam day-spending too long on one hard item can cost you easy points later.

Practicing under the clock is what builds reliable time management, not just content knowledge.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Complete at least one full timed randomized mock exam under strict real-exam conditions before sitting the actual certification.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Why version control matters

FHIR has multiple published versions (DSTU2, STU3, R4, R4B, R5) with real structural differences.

The mock exam's question bank is deliberately scoped and version-controlled to R4 so practice matches what the certification actually tests.

Slide 2: What gets excluded

  • Resources or elements introduced only in R5 (e.g., certain R5-only resource types)
  • Elements renamed or restructured between R4 and R5
  • Deprecated STU3 and DSTU2-only patterns no longer valid in R4

Slide 3: How it's maintained

Each question is tagged to its source spec version and periodically re-validated as the bank grows, preventing version drift from creeping into the practice content.

Slide 4: Exam focus

If an answer choice relies on R5-only behavior, it is the wrong answer on an R4-scoped certification exam.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Two modes, two purposes

Mock examinations offer two feedback modes so you can choose between fast learning and realistic simulation.

Slide 2: Immediate mode

Immediate mode tells you right after each question whether you were correct and shows the rationale immediately-useful early in preparation for quickly correcting misunderstandings.

Slide 3: Exam mode

Exam mode hides all feedback until you submit the entire mock exam, just like the real certification test.

This is the more accurate readiness signal because it removes the psychological safety net of instant confirmation.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Rely on exam mode results, not immediate-mode results, when judging whether you're actually ready to sit the real exam.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Beyond right or wrong

A mock exam score alone doesn't teach you much; the real learning happens in the detailed rationale attached to each question afterward.

Slide 2: What the rationale includes

  • Why the correct answer is right
  • Why each distractor is wrong (a common exam-writing technique worth studying)
  • A direct link to the relevant FHIR R4 specification page for further reading

Slide 3: How to use it

Review rationales for every question after an exam mode attempt-including ones you got right, since a correct guess built on a wrong assumption will resurface as a wrong answer later.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Following the specification links in rationales doubles as practice for scenario and navigation-style questions elsewhere in the certification program.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: What the dashboard shows

The readiness dashboard is an analytics view, not a lab-it combines four metrics gathered from your quizzes, mock exams, and lab activity into one picture of certification readiness.

Slide 2: Accuracy and confidence trend

  • Accuracy - percentage of questions answered correctly, shown overall and broken down by domain
  • Confidence trend - compares your self-rated confidence (before seeing the answer) against actual correctness over time, revealing overconfidence or underconfidence patterns

Slide 3: Time and lab completion

  • Time - average time spent per question or domain, compared against the real exam's time budget, to flag pacing problems
  • Lab completion - the percentage of hands-on labs finished, since practical resource-building skill isn't captured by quiz accuracy alone

Slide 4: Exam focus

Treat all four metrics together: strong accuracy with poor pacing or incomplete labs still means you are not fully exam-ready.

sections.detail:
Slide 1: Beyond a single score

A single accuracy percentage hides where the actual gaps are. The dashboard's heat maps break performance down visually so weak spots are easy to spot at a glance.

Slide 2: Misconception heat map

This view clusters your wrong answers by underlying misconception rather than by individual question-for example, repeatedly confusing Observation with DiagnosticReport shows up as one concentrated hot spot instead of several unrelated misses.

Slide 3: Weak-resource heat map

This view ranks resources or domains (e.g., Medication resources, terminology binding, RESTful search) by error rate, using color intensity to show where mistakes concentrate most.

Slide 4: Exam focus

Use the heat maps to direct final review time at the darkest cells first-fixing a shared misconception often clears several related wrong answers at once.
